comparative_notes: 3. Bng. poet. ɔiśu, ɔśu, Kṭg. and Kc. áśśu, Garh. “ãĩṣu” (Catak [1959: 45]) but aisu (Purohit and Benjwal) all ‘this year’, Gadd. axō ‘this year’ and axokā ‘of this year’, Dari. asau ‘this year’ < OIA aiṣámaḥ ‘in this year’ (2537) with no MIA parallels but modern parallels mostly in the northwest (note also Pal. heeṇṣúka ‘this year’), with the exception of Or. Note also the peculiar form youmus ‘this year’ in Pog. The word is used, for instance, in the à̄rul song of the hero Dzitu Dzɔṛiāṇ in the following verse: ki na aśia, boiɛ, dzitu dɔlu le dziɛ aĩseṇa na pɔṛɛ beṛu khi daṛɛ ɔiśu kɛ, boiɛli, bɔsteṇa ĩĩĩ, boiɛle, gabɛlu bɔriṇɛ, aĩ le, baṛɛ that not come.PR.3.SG.F, mother.VOC, Dzitu Dalu FIL heart.OBL problems yet fall.PR.3.PL sheep for.POP burr grass this year GEN.POP, mother.VOC FIL mother.VOC lamb fill.PP sheepfold ‘(Otherwise the hero) Dzitu (and his father) Dalu would have no matters near to their hearts, (and) (the wool of) the sheep would be (full with) burr grass,  (and), oh mother, this year’s cultivation of the fields (could be done), (and), oh mother, there would be sheepfolds filled with lambs.’

comparative_notes: 379. Bng. kvã̄sɔ ‘man’, Jaun. kvasa ‘boy’, Kann. and Him. khvās ‘concubine (of raja)’, and probably Bhad. kuānsh ‘wife’ (Kaul [2006 ii: 38]) (but cf. The forms are related with OIA lex. kumbhā- ‘harlot’ (3315) where Turner quotes Thieme according to whom the OIA word “is hypochoristic for kumbhadāsī- ‘harlot’. The Kann. and Him. words apparently derive < OIA kumbhadāsī- (with fronting of aspiration) whereas the Bng. and Jaun. forms are < OIA kumbhadāsa- with an original meaning something like *‘pimp’.

comparative_notes: 636. Ku. poet. ṭhula dəda ‘elder brother’, ṭhula kəka ‘elder uncle’, ṭhulo baba ‘anybody older than grandfather’ with first word < OIA sthūlá- ‘large, thick, stout’ (13776) which has the following semantic parallels in the northwest and west: Ind. ghʌ̀ṽ bà̄ ‘grandfather’, Gau. ghȭ̀ ẓhⁱũ̄ ‘elder/eldest brother’ and ghȭ̀ bà̄ ‘grandfather’, Bshk. gäṇ ‘big, elder’, Sv. ghaṇyeṛo ‘elder’, Paš. gaṇ-ayōm ‘my grand-mother’, Kal. gáḍa bába ‘older sister’ and gáḍa báya ‘older brother’, Kt. gaṇvóv ‘any male relative 4 gen- erations above Ego’, K. göḍañuku bōyu ‘elder brother’, Pr. gəndar ya ‘grandfather’ — Gadd. and Pāḍ. mōṭā puttar ‘elder son’, Garh. baṛā ‘father’s elder brother’, baṛī ‘wife of father’s elder brother’, Sad. bʌḍa ‘father’s elder brother’ and bʌḍi ‘mother’s elder sister’ — G. mōṭā bhaï ‘elder brother’ (LSI ix,ii: 406), M.wār. moṭay ‘father’s mother’ and moṭeba ‘father’s elder brother’ all either < OIA ghaná-² ‘compact, firm dense’ (4424) (Ind. and Gau.) or its allomorph *ghaṇḍa- or, in case of G., Gadd. and Pāḍ. < *moṭṭa-¹ ‘defective’ (10187) or, in case of Garh. and Sad. < OIA vaṛa- ‘big’ which is, however, cognate with vr̥ddhá- ‘large; old’. There is also a semantic parallel in the very east: B.chit. ṭɔ̀̄rda ‘grandfather’ (Učida [1970: 14]) with first component < OIA sthaurá- *‘strong’ (13780) (with a doubtful modern parallel in Dardic). This is a case of intra Indo-Aryan ‘calques’ (see p. 222). Note: Semantically different is Kho. lˈoṭ bap ‘great-grandfather’ and lˈoṭ vav ‘great-grandmother’ ← lˈoṭ ‘big’ which Strand derives < OIA laṭṭa- ‘bad man’ (10917), which has in some reflexes the meaning ‘old, worn-out’.

comparative_notes: 800. Gadd. nacrohī ‘the fourth day’ and nakarj ‘day before the day before yesterday’: both seem to begin with the same ‘prefix’ as found in H. narsõ ‘three days hence or before’; nakarj has a close morphological parallel in N. nikorsi ‘three days hence’ which Turner has placed sub OIA paraśvas ‘the day after tomorrow’ (7799j); further relationship with or influence through OIA *anutr̥tīyam ‘on the third day’ (318), OIA *ātr̥tīyam ‘on the third (day) back or forward’ (1130) and OIA tr̥tīya- ‘third’ (5912) are possible but hard to disentangle.

comparative_notes: 1034. Kgr. prasan ‘thread as it is spun’. T. Grahame Bailey tentatively suggests derivation < OIA “prasarana” (1908: 51), but more likely is derivation < OIA *prasevana- ‘twining’; cf. OIA prasiv- ‘to sew up’ and sub OIA sevana- ‘sewing’ (13443) dialectal Paš. sevanā ‘thread’. comparative_notes: 1067. Bng. phusi n.f. ‘female genitals’, Kṭg. and Kc. phʊ́ssi, phʊ́śṭi ‘female genitals’, Him. fusi, Paṭṭ. phəṣu ‘vagina’, Kann. phēċ ‘vagina’ — Bur. pháṣi ‘whore; woman, who is continuously coming and going’, Bur.ng. phóṣi ‘vagina’, Paš. phisū ‘vulva’ and perhaps Kal. kaphusi ‘witch’ (with a negative prefix) and Brah. pas ‘pudendum’. According to Turner (see Addenda and Corrigenda) < OIA *phussa- ‘defective’ (9100) and *phissa- ‘defective’ (9081), but this cannot be correct. There is also Gadd. pussī ‘darling’, but a possible connection with OIA *puśśī- ‘cat’ (8298) in a way comparable to English pussy ‘cat; female genitals’ (with parallels in other European languages) is not cor- roborated by Baṅgāṇī language consultants. According to Southworth (2005b: 13), this lemma may actually be a borrowing from Dravidian pucci ‘vulva’ as also found in M. pucci; however, there are also Southern Kiranti Bantawa phu ci ‘vulva, vagina’ and West Himalayish Kann. phɛ̄ċ ‘vulva’. An ex. from the Mid-West Himalayas: the beginning of a regionally well-known song which is sung in the night of the carnival-like ‘Old Diwali’ festival about a girl named Sungri: sungri ɛ phusɛ kɛ pã̄sru pelɛ kɛ gāṇḍi - cũ̄ cā Sungri hey pussy at ribbon penis at bell ring ring ‘hey Sungri, at your pussy is a ribbon at (the boy’s) penis is a bell - ding dong’

comparative_notes: 1127. Gadd. balnā ‘to speak’ < OIA Dhātup. bhálate ‘expounds, describes’ (9406) with a modern parallel in Ash. bel- ‘to speak’. Here in addition: Paš. phal ‘word’ and Bng. bùlṇɔ1 ‘to concentrate on s.th., be intensively busy with s.th.’, bùlɔndɔ ‘busy’ and bùlaṇɔ ‘to describe, explain’ — Ko.chr. bɔlmɛ̃ ‘sooth-saying’ and with Ira- nian agent suffix Ko. bolmeagār ‘magician’ with loss of aspiration, B. bhēlᵃkī ‘magic’ (ODBL § 281), Mult. “mūlā dā phull” ‘a charm to avert mūlā (a blight)’ (O’Brien [1881: 85]) (with loss of voice and a > u – quoted again p. 843)  where the “-ll-” in “phull” ‘charm’ suggests a dental lateral and thus, as in Bng., possibly deriva- tion < OIA *bhalyate. In Kal. one finds morphologically and semantically similar umbuḷík ‘to be possessed by a spirit (this is used to refer to a shaman’s action when possessed. During this time he will prophesy about the future)’ which could derive < OIA *udbhalate but much more likely is in this case Austro-Asiatic origin (see p. 980 sub ‘epilepsy’). Notes: The idea that the OIA root BHAL ‘attend to, observe’ may have developed < OIA SMR̥ ‘remember’ – for Mayrhofer BHAL . . . is probablt Middle Indo-Aryan for smārayo. . . (EWA) – is unlikely vis-à-vis the presented semantics and the fact that ‘remember’ is found in Bshk. as “shimeroo-” (Biddulph); however, note Pk. (Deś.) bhariyaṁ ‘remembered’. On the other hand, Pokorny’s suggestion that the OIA root derives < PIE *bhel- ‘schallen, reden, brüllen, bellen; resound, bark’ was apparently not accepted. As already noted above, Turner quotes sub OIA bhálate ‘expounds, describes’ (9406) Ash. bel- ‘to speak’. Addition- ally, Pokorny suggests – also without finding broader acceptance – the following two OIA words as reflexes of the PIE root *bhel- : bhá̄ṣate ‘speaks, says’ < PIE *bhel-s- and bháṇḍate ‘reproves, mocks, jests’ (9372) < PIE *bhel-n-do. Without wanting to question the difficulties found in Pokorny’s suggestion, it is worthwhile to look a little closer on modern reflexes of the two OIA verbs: (a) Modern reflexes in Outer Languages connected with the first OIA verb par- tially deviate from those found sub 9478 (bhá̄ṣate) and 9479 (bhāṣā-): Bng. bùśɛ laṇɔ ‘to talk, gossip, discuss’, Kṭg. búś and Kc. būś ‘chat, talk’, Ind. bhaṣáṽ ‘to scold’, Kal. baṣíkik ‘to boast, praise oneself’, Bhaṭ. bhaṣy ‘to talk trash’ and Ko. bās khā ‘to get a scolding; to scold; to prate’. Only West Pahāṛī Roh. bhāśṇõ ‘to promise’, quoted sub 9474, is semantically close to Medieval In- scriptional Pahāṛī, e.g. in tatsama shape Western Nepali bhāṣ (Pant [2009: 311]) and tadbhava Kumaoni paśā (M. P. Joshi [2009: 340f.]) both meaning ‘procla- mation’ or again in tatsama shape Kumaoni bhāṣa ‘bond’ (Pant loc. cit.). Neither these official-legal meanings nor several of the other here-quoted modern meanings match semantically with OIA bhāṣā- ‘speech, language (esp. common or vernacular speech, as opp. to Vedic or in later times to Sanskrit)’. However, only with Yājñavalkya and Dhūrtasamāgama the comparable meanings ‘(in law) accusation, charge, complaint, plaint’ are documented. This suggests that these meanings from the official-legal sphere are old but regionally limited. Moreover, meanings like Kal. baṣíkik ‘to boast, praise oneself’ can be due to contamination with reflexes of OIA vá̄śyate ‘roars, howls’ (11589) which is also reflected e.g. in Rom. bašaldo ‘musician’ (see p. 579). (b) The modern reflexes of OIA bhaṇḍa-² ‘jester, mime’, lex. bhāṇḍa-² ‘mimicry’ and bháṇḍate ‘reproves, mocks, jests’ (9372) quoted by Turner do not show the official-ritual contexts in which these words can be found.

comparative_notes: 1231. M.kuḍ. bhal ‘the beam of the ceiling’, Him. bhlaiṭhā ‘the main beam of a roof’ (which is probably a synonym compound with second component either < OIA stú̄pa- ‘main beam of house’ [13710] or < OIA sthú̄ṇā- ‘post, pillar’ [13774]) and bó̄ḷ ‘a high wooded place’ and possibly (without clear origin of first component) cēväḷ ‘a beam, of timber’, Kgr. bḷelū ‘the roof beam’ and perhaps P. barral ‘a beam on which the ceiling is supported’, Brj.-Aw. barīṇḍɔ ‘the ridgepole of a house; support’ is very similar to Gadd. “baranda” ‘ridgepole’ (Handa [2005: 191]) and to Gaw. balantˈə ‘main roof-beam’ (Morgenstierne [1950: 59]), Bi. bãṛerā and H. balẽṛī both ‘the ridgepole of a house’ (McGregor suggests for the H. word derivation < OIA *balidaṇḍa- probably basically meaning ‘strong stick’), cf. also Mj. vɔr ‘main roof-beam’ (Morgenstierne [1966: 186]), Yid. wāṛ ‘main roof-beam’, Sang. wāḷ ‘roof-beam’; Bng. bɔ̀ruāṇ n.f. ‘supporting beam at room ceiling’ (with -āṇ suffix?) and perhaps bàṭṭhɔ n.m. ‘supporting beam’ (with -(i)aṭhɔ suffix and loss of lateral?) (but the Bng. forms are close to OIA bhára- ‘carrying’ [9393] with unusual meaning shared with Ku. poet. bhəraṇə ‘central beam in roof’); cf. also IEW: 122 PIE *bʰel- ‘mostly with -ǵ- (-ḱ-) suffix ‘plank, beam” and Pk. (Deś.) belī- ‘post’; Čašule (e.g., 1998: 22) derives from this PIE lemma Bur. balk ‘plank, board, shelf’ but which also compares with Brah. palk ‘plank’ (with devoicing of initial consonant?); derivation or contamination of some of the forms < OIA vala- ‘beam’ is likely.

comparative_notes: 1292. Marw. mekhḷɔ ‘apron’, Rj. mekhalyo ‘a child’s dress’ — Bng. mekhḷɔ ‘belt’, Gadd. mekhala ‘waistband’ (Handa [2005: 80]), Garh. mekhḷu ‘long and loose shirt (which gets girdled)’. OIA mékhala- has the meanings ‘girdle, band, fillet; the edge or slope of a mountain’. There is also Garh. mekhlā ‘a (woman’s) girdle; slope surrounding a mountain, a string surrounding the middle part of any thing, zone, range’. The OIA word (see 10301) is of unknown origin and thus may be a ‘North Indian’ word. Some of the quoted modern forms may be tatsamas.

comparative_notes: 1393. Bro. lodo, ˈloðo ‘red’, Gaw. lutrʌ ‘red’, Gadd. lodha ‘blood’ respectively lodhā ‘blood of an animal’ (Wilson [1899a: xlvi]) are not directly < OIA lodhra- ‘the tree Symplocos racemosa (red bark of which is used for dyeing)’ (11139) (Pa., Pk.) but < OIA *lodhra- ‘red’. This is supported by G. lōḍ(h)ũ̄ ‘iron’. But there is also West Pahāṛī lodar ‘Symplocos cretaegoides’ (Handa [1998: 135]). Cf. also Sogdian rōðenē ‘of copper’, OIA *rodhra- ‘red’ (11139) with modern reflexes in K., S. and N. to which P. rudhar, rudhir ‘blood’ is to be added; origin of OIA lodhá- is not clear for Mayrhofer. Cf. also Jaṭ. ludhṛā ‘otter’ (p. 710) and Pr. ẓulō ‘copper’.

comparative_notes: 1416. Sub OIA vātaṁdhama- ‘blowing out wind’ (11492) and *vātadhmāna- ‘blowing of wind’ (11494) Turner lists Dm. bấdum ‘wind’ and dialectal Paš. vādana ‘wind’. The latter is quoted under both lemmata, indicating that also in case of the following addi- tional parallels it is usually not easy to reconstruct precisely the original lemma. But the following words also seem to be cognate: Chin. bāūdu ‘wind’, Kul. biānnā ‘wind’, Karak variety of Psht. bʌdʌme ‘wind’, Tir. bāni ‘wind’, Gaw. vádimon, vādiman ‘wind’ and Treg. vadamˈa ‘wind’. Slightly more distant looks Khet. buthān ‘air’ which seems to have close parallels in Rp. bətɔ̃ ‘wind’ and Garh. bəthɔ̃ ‘(strong) wind’. Note: Regarding phonetic development of the Kul. initial vowel -i- cf. OAw. bayāri ‘wind’ which is < OIA vātālī- ‘whirlwind’ (11500) for which there is a similar form in Cam., Kgr., Gadd. and Bhaṭe. biār, Cur. byār all ‘wind’ which, however, are < OIA *vātāra- (11497).

senses.definition_en: a person born while it was snowing
senses.definition_as: বৰফ পৰাৰ সময়ত জন্ম হোৱা ব্যক্তি

comparative_notes: 1498. Rudh. śina is used in impersonal phrases as śine ˈlʌora ‘it snows’ (Kaul [2006 ii: 274]) but the correct meaning is ‘it snowed’, K. śīn ‘snow’, Gadd. sinuri ‘a person born while it was snowing’ (a ‘totemic’ designation for a member of a subcaste of the Rāṭhī gotra [Shashi 1977: 41, 131]); the words derive < OIA snih- ‘wetness, moisture’ (13798) with a local parallel in Kṭg. sínnhɔ ‘wet’. Besides Rudh., K. and some other northwestern languages the old meaning ‘snow’ was only preserved in Pk. siṇēha- and perhaps in M.kuḍ. suno ‘snow’; the meaning is also found in Av. snij- ‘to snow’.

comparative_notes: 4. Bng. ɔ̀ḷkhiṇɔ ‘to give birth’ (with -i- grammeme) and ɔ̀ḷkhuari n.f. ‘midwife’ (with -ari grammeme), Deog. hɔḷkhioṇɔ ‘to give birth’, Khaśdh. hɔḷkhaṇa ‘to give birth’, Him. khlāi ‘a nurse’ (T. R. Joshi) — Bur. halḱ- ‘to give birth, drop (of an animal), have young ones’ and halkíṣ ‘womb’, Kal. halík ‘to bear a child’ (perhaps dissociated from older *halkík, but dental lateral is unclear) which is quoted under OIA á̄labhate ‘takes hold of’ (1362) with the meaning ‘bring’ but rightly described by Turner as “doubt- ful”. Here probably also belong Sir.shim. and Insir. haḷkā ‘child’, Gadd. halaṛu ‘son’, similar forms of which are also found in many varieties of Psht., e.g. in the Peshawar variety hʌˈlʌk ‘boy’. According to some speakers of West Pahāṛī, the basic meaning of the verb is ‘to become two parts, to divide’ (e.g. in birth or after convalescence when the disease has ‘left’ the person). An ex. from Bng.: meri ċhevēṛ rɔi ɔ̀ḷkhi, maĩ rɔi ɔi my wife remain.PP.F.SG deliver.VS, girl remain.PP.F.SG be.VS ‘my wife has delivered, a girl was (born)’

comparative_notes: 24. Bng. poet. purɔ n.m. ‘son, offspring’ and pur-khɛ lit. n.m.pl. ‘son-folk’ — G. pōryā ‘sons’, M. por(gā/gi) ‘child’ (also Gadd. porte ‘son’?), Ko. pōr ‘orphan’. comparative_notes: 104. Kgr. pukkā (also Maṇḍ.), pokā ‘kiss’, Gadd. and Cur. phōkū ‘kiss(es)’, Central Pahāṛī (Ku.) bhukki, bhuki ‘kiss’ (Sharma [1983: 75]), Garh. bhukkī ‘kiss; cheek’, Sirm. pŏkṭī ‘kiss’, Haṇḍūrī dialect of Kiũṭh. pūkā ‘kiss’, Pang. and Pāḍ. phă̄cī ‘kisses’ — Ind. pòk- pokʰ karʌ́ṽ ‘to produce a kissing sound’, Bur. poq ét- ‘to make a kissing sound’, Sh. pok-pók ‘ditto’ — Marw. bakō and Rj.mal. bōkō ‘kiss’, Bhil. poet. buskā devā ‘to kiss’ — Nih. bukki ‘kiss’ — Brah. buk ‘kiss’. Here probably also Sh.gil. “ma bòtze” ‘kiss’ (Leitner), bōtsȋ ‘ditto’, Bro. bōšē ‘kisses’, Tor. and Klm. bēs ‘kiss’, Dir. “pùch de” ‘give a kiss”, Paš. pačū ‘kiss’ (see also note [a] below), Kho. bočhík ‘to kiss’ — Orm. pọ̄č ‘kiss’ — Gaw. poṭe-θlites ‘kissed’ (LSI [viii, ii: 87]) resembles Chatt. poṭār-ke ‘having embraced’ (LSI [i,i: 238]), K. pūtu ‘kiss’ and similar Kt. patati ‘having kissed’ (Morgenstierne [1929a: 275], not found with Strand), Ind. ˈbūīčh ‘kiss’, Pal. búusi ‘kiss’, Sh. bóċo in bóċeṭ va-, bóċyeṭ va- ‘to meet ‘to come for a single kiss” and bóoċi ‘kiss’, K. bōsa, Pr. ā-picō-kso ‘he kissed’ (LSI [viii, ii: 64, 66]) and apič, apüč- ‘to kiss’, Kt. spč- or sapčé- or supči- ‘to kiss’, Kal. išpaḍék ‘to kiss’ and saváž hik ‘to kiss’ the latter of which has a parallel in Bashg. supča ‘kiss’ — probably Bro. čipādis ‘to kiss’ (with -dis ‘to give’) and Psht. čapaī ‘kiss’ (cf. with metathesis H. paccī ‘kiss’) — G. buccī and basī ‘kiss’, Him. bhũcu ‘sucked or licked’, Garh. pucārnu ‘to kiss, caress, fondle’, Rj.ajm. bācyō ‘kiss’, Bhil. bōkī ‘kiss’ (LSI [ix: 37]), bācyā ‘kisses’ (LSI [ix: 33]), bōsī ‘kisses’ (LSI [ix: 16]), P. and H. bosā ‘kiss’ and Ko.kaṇ. bos ‘kiss’ (all three ‘borrowings’ from Pers. bos ‘a kiss’, buss (in comp.) ‘kissing’).  Notes: (a) Indirectly connected are also Paš. muču and māṣˈū both ‘kiss’ (which also has čapū ‘kiss’), Sh.gur. māči ‘kiss’, Khaś. muċākā ‘smacking of lips or a hearty kiss sound’, H. macchī ‘kiss, buss’, Psht. mača and Par. mačī both ‘kiss’ which are borrowings ← Pers. māč. K. myūṭhu ‘kiss’, N. mukh miṭhyāuni ‘to smack the lips’ and note Pur. mikhi ‘kiss’ and Munda Kor. mukka ‘kiss’ — Rj.mal. maṭṭī ‘kiss’, G. mukkō ‘kiss’, M. mukā and Jaṭ. makho ‘a kiss’, Bhil. mukō, makū ‘kiss’, P. miṭṭhī, S. miṭhī, G. mīṭhī, M.kas. mutti all ‘kiss’. In addition Kul. māpī ‘kisses’ and In.sir. mughī ‘kisses’. Cf. also Ta. muttu ‘kiss’. (b) Some more distantly related allomorphs are H. babbī ‘kiss’, Td. pɔ, po ‘a kiss’, Jaṭ. happā, happī ‘kiss’ and similar B.roh. appá and appwá ‘kiss’, Kann. papu ‘kiss’ and Psht. pupaī ‘a kiss on the cheek’; Kṭg. bhòbəṛ and Him. bhubri both ‘mouth (contemptous)’ — P. būbā ‘the mouth, the face of a child’ — Kal. biv ‘mouth’. (c) Similar sounding Deshi Prakrit muddā and budī ‘kiss’ (Bhayani [1988: 36]) are ← Dravidian, cf. e.g. above-quoted Ta. muttu, muttam ‘kiss’ (DEDR 4960). (d) Many IE and other languages contain a word for ‘kiss’ beginning with bu- or pu- (IEW: 103 PIE *bu- ‘lip, kiss’), some also with mu-, plus an affricate or a sibilant, pointing to onomatopoeic origin: Middle Ir. bus, pus ‘lip’, busóc, pusóc ‘kiss’, Modern Pers. bōsīdan, Lith. bučiúoti ‘to kiss’, German Buss(i), English buss, Swedish puss, Latin basium, French baiser, bec, Galician bico ‘kiss’, Zaz. p’a č‘kiss’ (with glottalized stop), etc. Several of these are derived by Pokorny < PIE *bu- ‘kiss’ ‘as imitation of the kiss sound’, cf. also PIE *pukˆ- ‘to en- close, press together’ with Albanian puth ‘kiss’. Even though there is a clear onomatopoeic background to the above ‘kiss’ words, it is remarkable that the forms found with Pokorny have in South Asia parallels almost only in the west and northwest, that is mostly in the Outer Languages whereas in the Inner Languages derivations < OIA cumba- ‘kissing’ (4868) prevail (but there is also much overlapping). This shows that there was an innovative introduction of an onomatopeic form in the Inner Languages – according to Southworth (2005a: 76) ← Proto-Dravidian *cu(m)ppu ‘to suck’ (DEDR 2621b) – which cannot be compared with forms outside this area. Therefore a PIE origin for the above- discussed forms cannot be excluded although they got hopelessly scrambled with indigenous forms. (e) Regardings Southworth’s claim of Dravidian origin for OIA cumba-, note, however, also the following Austro-Asiatic words: Bahnaric Tampuan cum ‘kiss’ and Katu cɛm ‘kiss, sniff’; Monic Nyah Kur hɤ́m ‘cuddle and kiss vigorously’, Car hamkuː ‘kiss’, Vietnamese ôm ‘kiss’, and Palaungic Danaw kᵊmu¹ ‘to kiss; to smell’. They strongly suggest ultimate Austro-Asiatic origin. Above forms beginning with m- like G. mukkō ‘kiss’, etc. have plenty of parallels in Bahnaric languages as e.g. in Laven, Cheng, Brao, Alak, Oi, Nyaheun muk all ‘kiss’. Stray cases of several of the above forms are also found in (adjacent) Tibeto-Burman languages.

comparative_notes: 135. Bng. bugṇɔ v.i. ‘to bend’, bugṇɔ̃ adj. ‘disheartened, depressed (lit. ‘bent’)’, bugi ‘(roundish) belly of child or kid, roundish small pot’ and bogḷɔ ‘(trouser) pocket; tobacco pouch’ do not derive, because of lack of tone, < OIA bhugna- ‘bent, crooked’ (9522) with Pa. bhogga- ‘bent’, Pk. bhugga- ‘bent, crooked’ and a modern parallel in Si. Instead, since the Bng. words have parallels, a separate derivation < PIE *weng- ‘bend’ (and not < OIA BHUJ¹ ‘bend’) is suggested because the meanings differ substantially from those found sub 9522 in the following words (frequently with a > u): Gadd. bagḷū ‘a Gaddi’s purse of untanned skin (for tobacco)’ (which is also found bor- rowed into Munda Sant. bugli ‘a small bag, a purse’ and Mu. bāguli ‘a purse, pouch’), M. boṅgā ‘protuberance of a gravid womb’, Medieval Ku. buṅg ‘a hilltop where a fort is situated’ and rāj buṅg ‘royal fort’ (N. N. Misra et al. [1994: 67], but the ac- tual incomplete line of the copper plate from which the phrase is taken reads ja  vuṅgā [p. 60]); however, UGK writes sub buṅgā ‘choṭe samājoṁ ke nivās sthān (koṭ) ke buṅgā kahā jātā thā – the dwelling places of small communities (fortress, citadel, stronghold, house surrounded by a wall) used to be called buṅgā’. According to the archaeologist M. P. Joshi (pers. comm.), buṅgā is a landed estate, sometimes fortified, surrounded by hills, usually by two hills; it is not necessarily situated on a hill top, because there are Kumaoni place names like buṅgā-chīnā where chīnā means ‘ridge of a hill’, so this compound would mean ‘a fortified place on a ridge’; moreover, near village Dangoli in the Katyur Valley there is a large tract of land used for growing rice and the rice is called buṅgā kī bāsmatī; Joshi mentions also a Kumaoni word list probably from the 19th Century in which buṅgā is rendered as ‘fort-like’. The word buṅgā is mentioned for the first time in Kumaoni in the 10th Century. Edwin T. Atkinson (1973 [1882]: 507) writes about the Kumaoni King Som Chand (953-974): “When Som Chand came to Kumaon he built the first home of the Chands on the fifteen-acre plot received by him from his father-in-law and called it Ráj-búnga, which subsequently gave place to the name Champáwat.” — Kal. bạṅ ‘opening’ obviously in the sense of ‘glade, clearing’ as the following example shows: šátara bạ́ṅuna pay mo lasái, tsatrumá tay tyen ‘don’t let the goats go into that opening, the Bashgali people will beat you’ — The basic meaning of the words is perhaps best expressed in Garh. buṅgcā ‘muṛkar gol banā huā – (s.th. that got) bent into (s.th.) circular’ which makes it likely that also the following words belong to the same lemma: Bng. bukċɔ/buksɔ1 ‘blown up, inflated (e.g., cheek)’ (with -ċɔ, -sɔ suffix), and perhaps the slightly differently pronounced buksɔ2 n.m. ‘renal area’; Deog. bukċɔ n.m. ‘a filled up and baggy item (e.g. as a bag), a thick swelling (e.g. after a fall)’ (but for another interpretation see p. 981), Chin. bogśā ‘wild black conical or round mushroom’ (Kaul [2006 ii: 39]), N. buṅgo ‘cone, pod’, Jaṭ. būṅgā ‘circular stack containing straw of wheat or any other broken straw’ and P. buṅgā ‘(i) the lofty peak in which an Akālī finishes his head dress’; (ii) ‘a house, especially one of the costly buildings erected by the sardars around the Golden temple in Amritsar’ and (iii) ‘mansion’. Note: It is unclear whether Garh. buṅgṛā ‘ox, bullock of dwarf variety’ and boṅgṛo ‘a dwarf animal’ are related here.

comparative_notes: 146. Kal. brúndik ‘to grind one’s teeth together; to chew something, to grind something with one’s teeth’ as in moč kahár kái, dandọ́yak brúndin ‘when men are angry they will grind their teeth’ is probably same as Bng. mɔnṇɔ, mɔndṇɔ ‘to step on s.th., crush, tread on; to tan’ and with intensive suffix mɔndṛiaṇɔ (meanings similar to the fol- lowing Bng. words), P. mandhāṛṇā, mindhṇā ‘to crush’ and perhaps Gadd. “mandua” ‘leather pouch’ (Handa [2005: 36f.]). The words hardly derive < OIA márdati respec- tively *mṛndati ‘pounds’ (9890) which have regular reflexes with slightly different meanings in Bng. mɔṇḍakɔ n.m. ‘beat of threshing’, usually in ek mɔṇḍakɔ ‘(with) one beat of threshing’ (i.e. ‘very quickly’) (with -akɔ suffix) and mãḍṇɔ1, mãṇḍṇɔ1 ‘to tan by stamping with one’s feet; to beat’ and cf. above etymologically related Garh. māndro ‘winnowing tray, sieve’ (p. 840); Pokorny and Köbler (but not Mallory and Adams) postulate PIE *men-² ‘to step, stamp on, press together’ with e.g. Lith. minù, mìnti ‘to tan hides’. Note also Greek ματέω ‘to tread’ which Beekes derives with ques- tion mark < PIE *men- (2010: 913). EWA rejects the old idea that this root would be found in OIA carmamná- ‘tanner’ and argues for assimilation of OIA MLAI ‘wither’ (see also FLII 20.1.188); but the meaning ‘tan’ has been preserved in Bng. Here are two separate Bng. lemmata, but whether they are two different historical reflexes of the same OIA lemma or whether one is a direct PIE reflex is not completely clear. Notes: (a) Homonymous Bng. mãḍṇɔ2, mãṇḍṇɔ2 ‘to look or hunt around for’ and mã̄ḍ2 ‘need, necessity, purpose’ as e.g. in mã̄ḍ thɔi deṇi ‘what’s the point (of this)’ (besides widespread mã̄ḍ1 ‘rice broth’ which is < OIA maṇḍá- ‘scum of boiled rice’ [9735]) continues OIA (W.) maṇḍa- ‘pith, essence’. (b) Cf. also Wkh. manditk (Bellew) ‘leather’ where Morgenstierne asks (IIFL xxxv: 529) whether this is the perfect of mānd- ‘rubbed, tanned’ but the root actually means ‘rub, shampoo’. (c) Here (i.e. related with márdati) also Kal. mudhí, mundhí ‘clay’ which cf. with OIA MRAD ‘make soft’ and Wg. mŭ̄k ‘yellow clay’ < OIA *mr̥tka- ‘earth’ (10284). (d) Garh. māndro ‘(ann sambandhī bartan) dhān sukhāne ke lie – food con- nected utensil for drying paddy’ is used by Bhatt (1975 [vikrama 2032]: 395) in the sense of ‘winnowing tray’ or ‘sieve’ and thus seems to be cognate with OIA márdati ‘pounds’ (9890) (regarding semantics see there Si. ‘clean rice from the husk’). For semantically different reflexes of the OIA lemma see p. 840.

comparative_notes: 3. *drakk- ‘drag’ (6613, 14627). Has modern reflexes in Paš., Gau., Sv., Phal., Sh., Woṭ., and most probably Tor. Regarding Tōrwālī, Turner writes (14627): “Tor. (Biddulph) žigal- (prob. for ẓigal-) rather than < *jhikk-.” This is certainly correct because of Ind. ẓhikʌ́ṽ and Gau. ẓikȭ́ ‘to pull, drag’, yet, CDIAL 6613, 14627 and 5384 (*jhikk- ‘bend, jerk’) seem to be etymologically related. Here to be added are Klm. läkant LH ‘(he) is pulling’ and besides just-mentioned Ind. ẓhikʌ́ṽ “to pull; to stretch s.th.; to drag, lead an animal; to absorb’ also Kal. ẓikán ‘cowhide thongs for fastening shep- herds’ footwear’ and Bng. jìkṇɔ ‘to pull, drag; to carry (load)’. The -kk- can either be a verbal extension, *d(h)ra-kk-, or display typical word-final devoicing; in both cases the forms can go back to PIE(NW) *dʰregʰ- ‘pull, tear (out)’ which, being related with *trek- etc., seems to include irregular allomorphs. Note also Kgr. and Gadd. dharīṛnū ‘to drag’, Ḍhu-kaṛ. dhrūītē ‘having dragged’ (T. Grahame Bailey [1908: 21]), P. dhrūṇā ‘to drag’ (T. Grahame Bailey [1938: 243]) and perhaps Cam. dhrūmṇā ‘to draw’ (T. Grahame Bailey [1908: 13]). Notes: (a) Cam. dhramṇā ‘to tread upon’ is perhaps < OIA drámati ‘runs’ )loc. cit.) with spontaneous aspiration. (b) CDIAL 5384 has also been borrowed into Munda Bon. ʈiʈʈira - ǰik- ‘to pull a tendon’ (SEAlang) with second word morphologically practically same as Tor., Ind., Gau., Kal. (‘thongs’!).
